flawed_step: Step 4: the claim that because no single-vertex move helps, no partition can have a larger cut. Nothing guarantees this; changing several vertices at once can raise the cut even when no single move does.
counterexample: Path P4 a-b-c-d with sides {a,d} | {b,c}. Cut edges: ab and cd, so the value is 2. Moving a or d gives 1. Moving b gives cut edges {bc, cd}, still 2, and moving c is symmetric. So no single move strictly increases the cut. But {a,c} | {b,d} cuts all 3 edges, so the maximum cut is 3 > 2.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
1. Let (S,T) be a partition where no single-vertex move strictly increases the cut. — Justified: this is the hypothesis.
2. For each vertex v, moving v changes the cut by (neighbours of v on v's own side) − (neighbours of v on the other side). So local optimality means every v has at least as many neighbours across the cut as on its own side. — Justified: direct count.
3. Adding step 2 over all v shows the cut value is at least |E|/2. — Justified: a standard, correct bound.
4. So (S,T) has the largest cut value among all partitions. — NOT justified. Step 3 only gives a lower bound of |E|/2, and step 2 only rules out single-vertex moves, not moves of several vertices. Counterexample: in the path a-b-c-d, {a,d}|{b,c} has cut value 2 and is locally optimal (moving a or d gives 1; moving b or c keeps 2). Yet {a,c}|{b,d} has cut value 3.
5. Conclusion: the partition is a maximum cut. — Not justified: it depends on step 4, and the counterexample shows the conclusion is false.
Verdict: the statement is false. A partition that no single move can improve need not be a maximum cut; it is only guaranteed to cut at least half the edges.
